00-the-path-of-a-request.q: What is the difference between north–south and east–west traffic?
options: Encrypted vs unencrypted traffic
Traffic between the outside world and your system vs traffic between your own services
Upload vs download
IPv4 vs IPv6
00-the-path-of-a-request.why: North–south crosses your edge (users, partners → your system); east–west stays inside (service to service). The tools differ: CDN/LB/gateway for north–south, service mesh for east–west.
whyWrong: Both directions can and should be encrypted — encryption isn't what the terms describe.
Direction of data transfer isn't the distinction; both kinds carry both.
The IP version is irrelevant to the north–south/east–west split.

00-the-path-of-a-request.q: Requests are still flowing normally, but no configuration change you make takes effect. Which half of the system is down?
options: The data plane
The control plane
DNS
The CDN
00-the-path-of-a-request.why: The data plane is whatever touches requests in flight; the control plane is whatever configures it. Flowing traffic + frozen config = data plane fine, control plane down.
whyWrong: If the data plane were down, requests would not be flowing.
If DNS were down, new connections would be failing, not config changes.
A CDN outage would show as failing or slow requests, not ignored config.

00-the-path-of-a-request.q: Why does the request path put the CDN before the load balancer?
options: CDNs are older technology, so they come first historically
The CDN's job is to answer as many requests as possible before they reach your infrastructure at all
Load balancers can't handle TLS
It's arbitrary; the order doesn't matter
00-the-path-of-a-request.why: The CDN is the outermost ring because a cache hit at the edge means your origin — including the load balancer — never sees the request. The cheapest request is the one that never arrives.
whyWrong: Age has nothing to do with placement; jobs determine order.
Load balancers terminate TLS routinely — that's not the reason.
The order is the point: each ring exists to shed work from the rings behind it.

01-load-balancers.q: What is the practical difference between an L4 and an L7 load balancer?
options: L7 is newer and faster
L4 sees connections (IPs and ports); L7 reads the request itself (path, headers) and can route on it
L4 is for internal traffic only
L7 requires special hardware
01-load-balancers.why: L4 forwards bytes between addresses without understanding them — fast and protocol-agnostic. L7 parses the protocol, so it can send /api/ one way and /images/ another, retry a GET, or split traffic for a canary.
whyWrong: L7 does more work per request — it's the slower, smarter one.
L4 balancers sit at the public edge of most large systems.
Both are ordinary software; Envoy does both on any machine.

01-load-balancers.q: Why are sticky sessions usually considered a design smell?
options: They're slower than round robin
They mean a server holds user state, so that server's death logs users out and servers stop being interchangeable
Browsers don't support them
They only work with IPv6
01-load-balancers.why: Stickiness exists to compensate for state living on one server. Move the state to a shared store and any server can answer, the balancer stays free to route anywhere, and a server dying is a non-event.
whyWrong: The routing cost is trivial; the architectural coupling is the problem.
Stickiness is implemented by the balancer (usually via cookie), and browsers handle cookies fine.
IP version has nothing to do with session affinity.

01-load-balancers.q: Your /healthz handler checks that the database is reachable. During a 30-second database blip, what does the load balancer do to your fleet?
options: Nothing — health checks don't run that often
It removes every server at once, because they all fail the same dependency check, turning a wobble into an outage
It doubles the traffic to compensate
It restarts the database
01-load-balancers.why: Every server reports the same dependency failure simultaneously, so the balancer drains the entire pool. Health checks should verify what the server itself controls; dependency health belongs in separate signals.
whyWrong: Checks typically run every few seconds — well within a 30-second blip.
Balancers don't create capacity or traffic; they only distribute what arrives.
A load balancer has no idea the database exists — it only sees the check fail.

02-api-gateways.q: Which of these belongs IN an API gateway?
options: Merging the orders and billing responses into one JSON for the mobile app
Skipping the fraud check for gold-tier customers
Validating tokens, enforcing rate limits, and routing /v2/ to the new service
Recalculating cart totals
02-api-gateways.why: Cross-cutting policy — authn at the edge, quotas, routing, TLS, observability — is exactly the front desk's job: every service would otherwise implement it identically.
whyWrong: Aggregation is an application; that's what a backend-for-frontend service is for.
Tier-based behavior is business logic — it changes when the product changes, so it belongs in a service someone owns.
Money math is core business logic; the gateway should never know what a cart is.

02-api-gateways.q: What was the ESB, and why does it come up in gateway discussions?
options: An early load balancer that couldn't do TLS
The enterprise service bus — middleware that gradually absorbed business logic until nobody could change anything; the cautionary tale for gateways
A Kubernetes component replaced by Ingress
A CDN feature for APIs
02-api-gateways.why: The ESB ate a generation of architectures by centralizing logic in shared middleware. A gateway that accumulates orchestration and business rules is rebuilding it in YAML — which is why the should-not list exists.
whyWrong: It wasn't a load balancer; it was integration middleware.
It predates Kubernetes and lived at a different layer entirely.
It has nothing to do with CDNs.

02-api-gateways.q: When does an INTERNAL gateway earn its place?
options: Always — every microservice should sit behind one
When a domain inside the company (say, a payments platform) is consumed by many other teams and needs stable routes, quotas, and an audit trail
Whenever you install a service mesh
When the external gateway is overloaded
02-api-gateways.why: An internal gateway makes sense when part of your system is effectively a product with internal customers. Short of that, an external gateway plus a mesh covers most architectures — an internal gateway earlier is premature machinery.
whyWrong: Per-service gateways everywhere is overhead without a matching problem — the mesh already handles east–west concerns.
A mesh reduces the need for internal gateways by providing mTLS, retries, and telemetry between services.
Capacity problems are solved by scaling the gateway, not adding a differently-purposed one.

03-cdns.q: A response marked Cache-Control: public contains the logged-in user's account details. What happens?
options: Nothing — CDNs know not to cache personal data
The edge may cache it and serve one user's account page to other users: a data breach
The response gets slower
The CDN encrypts it extra
03-cdns.why: Shared caches do what the headers say. 'public' on a per-user response invites the edge to store it under a key other users will hit. Personal responses need private/no-store — and a review process for cache headers.
whyWrong: CDNs cannot know what's personal; the headers are the contract, and they said public.
Speed isn't the issue — disclosure is.
Encryption on the wire doesn't help; the cache serves the decrypted response to the wrong person.

03-cdns.q: Why do frontend builds name files like app.9f31c2.js instead of app.js?
options: Shorter names load faster
The hash hides the code from competitors
A new deploy produces a new URL, so old cached copies never conflict — caching can be maximal and invalidation becomes unnecessary
It's required by JavaScript modules
03-cdns.why: Versioned URLs dissolve the invalidation problem: the immutable file is cached for a year, and 'updating' is just referencing a new name. Rollback is the old name. Nothing needs purging, ever.
whyWrong: The name is longer, not shorter — and length is irrelevant.
The content is exactly as public as before; the hash is a version stamp, not obfuscation.
No module system requires hashed names; build tools add them for caching.

03-cdns.q: For which of these is a CDN the WRONG tool?
options: A product-image gallery served worldwide
Absorbing a traffic spike on a viral blog post
Reading an account balance immediately after a transfer
Serving yesterday's leaderboard to millions
03-cdns.why: A balance-after-write is a strong-consistency read: it must come from the system of record. A cache is by definition allowed to be stale — that's the deal that makes it fast.
whyWrong: Static images for a global audience are the CDN's founding use case.
Identical cacheable content under read spike is exactly what edge caching absorbs.
Slightly-stale, identical-for-everyone content is ideal CDN material.

04-dns-and-tls.q: You updated a DNS record to point at the new server, but half your users still reach the old one hours later. Why?
options: DNS servers are slow to process changes
Resolvers cached the old answer and will keep it until its TTL expires — and some ignore TTLs entirely
The new server rejected the record
You need to restart the old server
04-dns-and-tls.why: DNS scales by caching at every step, and a cached answer lives for its TTL regardless of what you changed upstream. That's why migrations lower TTLs the day before, and why serious failover uses anycast instead of racing caches.
whyWrong: Authoritative servers pick up the change quickly — the delay lives in everyone else's caches.
Servers don't accept or reject DNS records; DNS is resolved by clients, not targets.
The old server has no say in where names point.

04-dns-and-tls.q: Your HTTPS site works in every browser but fails from curl and a Java service with certificate errors. The likely cause?
options: curl doesn't support TLS
The server sends an incomplete certificate chain; browsers repair missing intermediates, strict clients don't
Java requires special certificates
The certificate expired
04-dns-and-tls.why: Browsers fetch missing intermediates automatically; most other clients validate exactly the chain the server presents. Serving the full chain fixes every client at once — this is the classic asymmetric TLS bug.
whyWrong: curl speaks TLS fine; it's just honest about broken chains.
Java validates the same standard chains — it simply doesn't repair yours.
An expired certificate fails everywhere, browsers included.

04-dns-and-tls.q: What does it mean to choose where TLS terminates?
options: Choosing when the certificate expires
Choosing which component decrypts the traffic — and therefore where plaintext begins inside your system
Choosing the cipher suite
Choosing between HTTP and HTTPS
04-dns-and-tls.why: Termination is the decryption point: edge-only termination means plaintext everywhere inside; hop-by-hop re-encryption and mesh mTLS push the trust boundary inward until every service proves its identity. It's a security architecture decision, not a checkbox.
whyWrong: Expiry is a certificate property, unrelated to the termination point.
Cipher choice happens at every TLS hop regardless of where you terminate.
That choice is whether to use TLS at all — termination is about where it ends.

05-queues-caches-async.q: Why must a queue consumer be idempotent?
options: To process messages faster
Because delivery is at-least-once in practice: the same message can arrive twice, and processing it twice must not double the effect
Because queues shuffle message order
Because messages expire
05-queues-caches-async.why: Redelivery after failures is part of the contract — exactly-once is a marketing word. Handlers keyed on 'have I already processed order 4412?' make duplicates harmless; handlers that charge on every delivery make them incidents.
whyWrong: Idempotence is about correctness under redelivery, not throughput.
Ordering is a separate concern; duplicates arrive even in strictly-ordered streams.
Expiry would mean fewer deliveries, not repeated ones.

05-queues-caches-async.q: A hot cache key expires and 5,000 concurrent requests hit the database at once. What is this called, and what's the fix?
options: A cache breach; rotate credentials
A stampede; stagger TTLs or let one request refresh while others briefly serve the stale value
Normal operation; databases handle it
A memory leak; restart the cache
05-queues-caches-async.why: The cache was hiding that load; simultaneous expiry returns it as a spike. Jittered TTLs spread the refreshes, and serve-stale-while-revalidate collapses 5,000 refreshes into one.
whyWrong: Nothing was breached — no attacker is involved, just an expiry.
The database sized for cached traffic meets uncached traffic — that's exactly the outage.
Memory is fine; the pattern is about expiry timing, not leaks.

05-queues-caches-async.q: Why should file uploads go directly from the browser to object storage via a pre-signed URL instead of through your application servers?
options: Browsers can't send files to application servers
It's more secure because the URL is secret forever
Application servers then never carry file traffic — the service issues a short-lived scoped link, stores the key, and stays out of the byte path
Object storage is the only place TLS works for files
05-queues-caches-async.why: Pass URLs, not bytes: the pre-signed link is short-lived and permission-scoped, the heavy transfer happens between the user and storage built for it, and your expensive stateless servers do what they're good at.
whyWrong: Browsers upload to app servers fine — it's just a waste of your compute and bandwidth.
Pre-signed URLs are deliberately short-lived; their security comes from scope and expiry, not permanent secrecy.
TLS works everywhere; that's not the differentiator.
